cards.front: Why is AC (not DC) used for power distribution?
cards.back: AC can be transformed. Stepping voltage up cuts current, so power travels long distances on smaller wire with less I²R loss.
cards.note: Doubling voltage halves current and cuts line loss to 1/4.

cards.front: Why won't a transformer work on steady DC?
cards.back: Only a CHANGING flux induces voltage. Steady DC makes constant flux, so nothing is induced, and the winding only sees its low resistance (it can overheat).
cards.note: Faraday's law: induced voltage depends on rate of change of flux.

cards.front: How is energy transferred from primary to secondary in a conventional transformer?
cards.back: Magnetically, through a shared changing flux in the iron core. There is no electrical connection between windings.
cards.note: Exception: the autotransformer, which shares one winding.

cards.front: In the classic two-coil demo, what happens to the lamp as the coils move closer, and when an iron core is added?
cards.back: It gets brighter both times. More of the primary's flux links the secondary (better coupling). Iron carries flux far more easily than air.
cards.note: Iron has high permeability.

cards.front: What mechanical device is a transformer most like?
cards.back: A gearbox. Gears trade speed for torque; a transformer trades voltage for current. Turns ratio = gear ratio, and power stays (almost) the same.
cards.note: Friction in gears ≈ core and copper losses.

cards.front: State the power rule that solves most transformer problems.
cards.back: Power in ≈ power out: EP × IP = ES × IS (VA in = VA out).
cards.note: If more VA comes out than goes in, your math is wrong.

cards.front: Which side of a transformer carries the higher current?
cards.back: The low-voltage side. High voltage side = low current.
cards.note: Check every current answer with a VA check.

cards.front: Higher voltage lets you use smaller conductors. What is the trade-off?
cards.back: Insulation and clearances. Higher voltage needs thicker insulation and more spacing.
cards.note: Conductor area needed for a given loss goes as 1/V².

cards.front: Power transformer vs distribution transformer?
cards.back: Power transformer: between generator and primary distribution (substations, large). Distribution transformer: from primary distribution (4–35 kV) to the customer's service (e.g., 120/240 V).

cards.front: Are 'primary' and 'secondary' fixed labels?
cards.back: No. Primary = the side the power enters. Feed a step-down unit from its low side and it becomes a step-up unit.
cards.note: H/X marks voltage level; primary/secondary marks power direction.

cards.front: Write the transformer EMF equation and define each term.
cards.back: E<sub>rms</sub> = 4.44 × f × N × Φ<sub>max</sub>. f = frequency (Hz), N = turns, Φmax = peak core flux (Wb).
cards.note: Every turn sees the same flux, so voltage per turn is the same on both windings.

cards.front: What happens if a 60 Hz transformer is run on 50 Hz at the same voltage?
cards.back: Flux rises about 20% (E = 4.44 f N Φ). The core can saturate, magnetizing current jumps, and it overheats.
cards.note: Overvoltage has the same effect.

cards.front: What is excitation (magnetizing) current?
cards.back: The small current the primary draws with no load, to magnetize the core. Typically a few percent of FLC or less, lagging voltage by nearly 90°.
cards.note: An unloaded transformer looks like an inductor.

cards.front: How does the primary 'know' that load was added to the secondary?
cards.back: Secondary current makes an opposing flux. The primary automatically draws more current to cancel it and keep core flux constant.
cards.note: The load sets the current; the transformer just passes it through.

cards.front: Why are transformer cores laminated?
cards.back: Thin, insulated silicon-steel sheets break up eddy-current paths, so the circulating currents (and their heat) stay small.
cards.note: Solid iron would act like a shorted turn.

cards.front: What are eddy currents?
cards.back: Circulating currents induced in the core iron itself by the changing flux. They waste power as heat.
cards.note: Reduced by thin insulated laminations.

cards.front: What is hysteresis loss, and how is it reduced?
cards.back: Energy lost each cycle re-magnetizing the iron. Reduced by using silicon steel with a narrow hysteresis loop.
cards.note: Hysteresis + eddy = core (iron) loss.

cards.front: Core form vs shell form construction?
cards.back: Core form: windings surround the core legs. Shell form: the core surrounds the windings.
cards.note: Core form is common on HV/large units; shell form on small units.

cards.front: Do air gaps in a transformer core increase its efficiency?
cards.back: No. Air gaps raise magnetizing current and lower efficiency. They're used deliberately in reactors, ballasts, neon and flyback transformers to store energy or limit current.

cards.front: Write the turns, voltage and current ratio equation.
cards.back: N<sub>P</sub>/N<sub>S</sub> = E<sub>P</sub>/E<sub>S</sub> = I<sub>S</sub>/I<sub>P</sub>
cards.note: Voltage goes WITH turns; current goes AGAINST turns.

cards.front: What is TTR?
cards.back: Transformer turns ratio: primary turns to secondary turns, usually written high side to low side (e.g., 10:1).
cards.note: Also the name of the field test that measures it.

cards.front: What is 'ampere-turns balance'?
cards.back: I<sub>P</sub> × N<sub>P</sub> = I<sub>S</sub> × N<sub>S</sub>. Primary ampere-turns equal secondary ampere-turns.
cards.note: Same as saying current ratio is the inverse of turns ratio.

cards.front: What is reflected impedance?
cards.back: The primary sees the load impedance times the turns ratio squared: Z<sub>P</sub> = (N<sub>P</sub>/N<sub>S</sub>)² × Z<sub>S</sub>.
cards.note: A 2 Ω load on a 10:1 transformer looks like 200 Ω from the primary.

cards.front: A winding is tapped. Which turns do you use to compute TTR?
cards.back: The whole winding, unless the problem says which tap is used. E.g., 2,400 V to a center-tapped 240 V winding = 10:1.

cards.front: At a fixed supply voltage, what happens to flux and secondary voltage if you add primary turns?
cards.back: At a fixed supply voltage, more primary turns means LESS flux and LOWER secondary voltage. Secondary current is set by the load.

cards.front: Name 8 items found on a transformer nameplate.
cards.back: Any 8: manufacturer, serial no., kVA, phases, frequency, HV and LV voltages, FLCs, temperature rise, %Z, polarity, connection diagram, tap table, cooling/insulation type, BIL, weight, oil volume.
cards.note: NEC 450.11 requires marking. The nameplate is a formal document.

cards.front: In '12,470 – 240', what does the dash mean?
cards.back: It separates the windings. First voltage = the side receiving power (primary), second = secondary.

cards.front: 120/240 vs 240/120: what's the difference?
cards.back: 120/240 = two separate 120 V coils (can be series for 3-wire or parallel). 240/120 = one 240 V coil with a center tap (3-wire only; can't parallel).
cards.note: Order matters!

cards.front: What ambient temperature are transformer ratings based on?
cards.back: 40 °C maximum (30 °C average over 24 h).

cards.front: Same kVA: 55 °C rise vs 65 °C rise unit. Which has more overload headroom?
cards.back: The 55 °C (lower-rise) unit. More copper/iron and better cooling: the 'young, healthy runner'.

cards.front: Besides load current, name 4 factors that limit transformer loading.
cards.back: Cooling medium, ambient temperature, duration of overloads, rated temperature rise, altitude (also harmonics, blocked vents, low oil).

cards.front: Overload vs fault?
cards.back: Overload: more than rated current through the normal path; damage is slow, from heat. Fault: current through an abnormal path, often many times rated; protection must clear it fast.
cards.note: An overload is NOT a fault.

cards.front: Why can a transformer tolerate short overloads?
cards.back: Thermal mass: temperature lags load by minutes to hours. Long overloads still age insulation fast (rule of thumb: life halves per ~8–10 °C over rating).

cards.front: Series vs parallel connection of a 120/240 V secondary (25 kVA)?
cards.back: Series (X2–X3 jumpered): 120/240 V 3-wire, 104 A. Parallel (X1–X3, X2–X4): 120 V 2-wire, 208 A.
cards.note: kVA is the same either way.

cards.front: Two secondary coils in series with one reversed: what happens?
cards.back: The voltages cancel: about 0 V instead of the sum.

cards.front: Does paralleling secondaries increase available kVA?
cards.back: No. It only changes how the available current is delivered (more amps at lower voltage).

cards.front: What should you inspect before accepting a transformer shipment?
cards.back: On the truck: damaged bushings, oil leaks, bulged/dented tank, broken gauges, overheating/arc signs, lead condition. Note damage before signing.

cards.front: Name 5 periodic transformer maintenance items.
cards.back: Keep records; maintain oil level; keep moisture out; keep parts clean/rust-free; test winding insulation and oil; lubricate moving parts; keep enclosures tight; check fans, arresters, gauges, grounds.

cards.front: What three sections make up a unit substation?
cards.back: High-voltage switch, dry-type transformer, secondary distribution section, all in one lineup.
cards.note: Often owner-furnished; common in industrial plants. Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: Core loss vs copper loss: which changes with load?
cards.back: Core (iron) loss is roughly constant whenever energized. Copper (I²R) loss rises with the square of load current.
cards.note: Max efficiency occurs where they're equal.

cards.front: Transformer efficiency formula and typical range?
cards.back: %Eff = P<sub>out</sub> ÷ P<sub>in</sub> × 100. Typically 96–99%.
cards.note: Among the most efficient machines made.

cards.front: Why does oversizing a transformer 'for safety' waste energy?
cards.back: Core loss is paid 24/7 whether loaded or not. A lightly loaded big unit runs at low efficiency.

cards.front: Why are transformers rated in VA, not watts?
cards.back: Heating depends on current, and current depends on VA regardless of power factor. A watt rating would let low-PF loads overheat the unit.
cards.note: 50 kW at PF 0.7 = 71.4 kVA vs 55.6 kVA at PF 0.9.

cards.front: FLC vs FLA?
cards.back: Same thing: full-load current/amps, the current the transformer can carry continuously at rated conditions.

cards.front: Single-phase full-load current formula?
cards.back: I<sub>FL</sub> = VA ÷ E = kVA × 1,000 ÷ E.
cards.note: Three-phase: divide by E × 1.732.

cards.front: How can you get the TTR from the full-load currents?
cards.back: Divide the secondary FLC by the primary FLC (high current ÷ low current).

cards.front: Single-phase amps-per-kVA rule of thumb?
cards.note: Rounded charts (4, 2, 0.4) read a few percent low.

cards.front: Name the common single-phase distribution transformer sizes.
What is the limitation of a load check with a clamp meter?
cards.back: It's a snapshot. Peak demand (hot afternoon, evening) matters more than a single reading.

cards.front: What is BIL?
cards.back: Basic Impulse Insulation Level: the peak lightning-type surge voltage (kV crest) the insulation can withstand without damage.
cards.note: Much higher than operating voltage, e.g., ~95 kV BIL for 15 kV-class gear.

cards.front: What is a dry-type transformer?
cards.back: A self air-cooled transformer: air circulates through vents in a sheet-metal case. Most indoor building transformers.

cards.front: Two jobs of oil in an oil-immersed transformer?
cards.back: Cooling (carries heat to tank and fins by convection) and insulation. It also keeps paper insulation from drying out and oxidizing.
cards.note: Mineral oil is flammable, so NEC Art. 450 Part II has stricter rules for it.

cards.front: How does natural convection cool an oil-filled transformer?
cards.back: Hot oil near the core rises (less dense), carries heat to the tank and radiators, cools, sinks, and returns.

cards.front: What does %Z mean on a transformer nameplate?
cards.back: The percent of rated primary voltage needed to push full-load current through a shorted secondary.
cards.note: Tells you fault current and voltage regulation.

cards.front: Why is transformer impedance given in percent instead of ohms?
cards.back: One number works for both sides. In ohms, HV and LV values differ (by the turns ratio squared).

cards.front: Maximum short-circuit current formula from %Z?
cards.back: ISC = IFL × 100 ÷ %Z (infinite source).
cards.note: Real fault current is somewhat lower; this is the worst case.

cards.front: Low %Z vs high %Z: trade-offs?
cards.back: Low %Z: better voltage regulation, but higher fault current (higher AIC and arc-flash). High %Z: limits fault current, but more voltage drop/dip under load.
cards.note: %Z is a design choice, not a quality grade.

cards.front: Liquid-filled transformers: name 4 liquids used today, and the liquid's two jobs.
cards.back: Mineral oil (combustible), silicone fluid, seed-oil (natural ester) coolants, other non-toxic high-dielectric liquids. Jobs: insulate HV from LV windings, and carry heat from core and coils to the tank/radiators/fans.
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: Advantages of dry-type over liquid-filled transformers?
cards.back: Lighter, simpler to install, no leak precautions or containment, no coolant replacement. Fans can be added to carry more load.
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: Why does the textbook multiply the marked %Z by 0.9 in fault calculations?
cards.back: Listed transformers ≥25 kVA have ±10% impedance tolerance. Actual %Z may be 10% lower, which means more fault current: the worst case.

cards.front: How do service conductors change the available fault current, and what method does the book use?
cards.back: Their impedance lowers it. Point-to-point method: f from length, conductor constant C and voltage; M = 1 ÷ (1 + f); I_end = I_start × M. Example: 34,725 A → about 30,558 A over 25 ft of 3 × 250 kcmil Cu in PVC.
cards.note: Textbook Problem 2, Ch. 18.

cards.front: Besides the transformer, what else adds to or raises available fault current?
cards.back: Motor contribution (running motors act as generators briefly) and higher system voltage (+10% V → +10% fault current).
cards.note: Book recommends interrupting ratings ≥25% above calculated. Textbook Ch. 18.

cards.front: What do H and X terminal markings mean?
cards.back: H = high-voltage terminals (H1, H2, H0...). X = low-voltage terminals (X1, X2, X0...).
cards.note: H/X is about voltage level, not which side is the primary.

cards.front: The basic polarity rule?
cards.back: H1 and X1 are positive at the same instant (H2 and X2 negative).

cards.front: Facing the low-voltage side, where is H1 normally?
cards.back: On your left (back-left bushing).

cards.front: Additive vs subtractive: where is X1?
cards.back: Subtractive: X1 on the SAME side as H1 ('same side subtractive'). Additive: X1 diagonally opposite H1.

cards.front: Can polarity be changed from outside the transformer?
cards.back: No. It's set by winding direction and how the leads are brought out. You connect to suit it.

cards.front: Which single-phase transformers are normally additive?
cards.back: Units of 200 kVA or less with HV of 8,660 V or less (ANSI C57.12.00). Larger or higher-voltage units are subtractive.
cards.note: Most pole-top distribution transformers are additive.

cards.front: Why is subtractive polarity preferred on large/HV units?
cards.back: Lower voltage stress between adjacent HV and LV leads: half the DIFFERENCE of the voltages vs half the SUM for additive.

cards.front: Can an additive and a subtractive transformer be paralleled?
cards.back: Yes, if you connect by H1/X1 markings (polarity), not by physical bushing position.

cards.front: Why does the kick test only deflect momentarily?
cards.back: Voltage is induced only while flux is changing (when current starts or stops). Steady DC = no induced voltage.
cards.note: Lenz/Faraday.

cards.front: Requirements for paralleling two transformers?
cards.back: Same voltage ratio (and tap), same/similar %Z, correct polarity; for 3Ø also same phase sequence and angular displacement.
cards.note: Mismatched ratio → circulating current even at no load. Mismatched %Z → unequal sharing.

cards.front: What current does the neutral of a 120/240 V 3-wire system carry?
cards.back: The DIFFERENCE between L1 and L2 currents (the unbalance). Balanced = 0 A.
cards.note: It is the difference between the leg currents, not their sum.

cards.front: Wye: relationship of line and phase voltage and current?
cards.back: EL = 1.732 × EP; IL = IP.
cards.note: E.g., 208 V line → 120 V phase.

cards.front: Delta: relationship of line and phase voltage and current?
cards.back: E<sub>L</sub> = E<sub>P</sub>; I<sub>L</sub> = 1.732 × I<sub>P</sub>.
cards.note: Phase current inside a delta can't be clamped from outside.

cards.front: Three-phase kVA formula?
cards.back: kVA = E<sub>L</sub> × I<sub>L</sub> × 1.732 ÷ 1,000.

cards.front: Forming a wye from three 1Ø cans: what gets connected together?
cards.back: The non-polarity terminals (H2s or X2s). That common point is the neutral; the polarity terminals become the lines.

cards.front: Forming a delta from three 1Ø cans?
cards.back: Polarity to non-polarity around the loop (X1 of A to X2 of B, etc.). No neutral.

cards.front: Advantages of three single-phase cans over one 3Ø tank?
cards.back: Replace one failed unit, keep one spare, run open-delta on two units (57.7% capacity).
cards.note: A single 3Ø tank is smaller, cheaper and more efficient.

cards.front: The four basic 3Ø transformer connections?
cards.back: Delta–delta, delta–wye, wye–delta, wye–wye.
cards.note: Delta–wye (e.g., 480 V → 208Y/120) is most common in buildings.

cards.front: What is an open-delta bank, and when is it used?
cards.back: Two transformers giving 3Ø (and 1Ø via a center tap on one). Used where the utility has only two primary phases nearby, for small 3Ø loads, or where a third unit will be added later.
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: 120/240 V 4-wire (high-leg) delta: voltages A–N, C–N, B–N, and phase-to-phase?
cards.back: A–N and C–N = 120 V; B–N = 208 V (high leg); every phase-to-phase = 240 V.
cards.note: B can't serve line-to-neutral loads.

cards.front: High-leg meter-socket trap?
cards.back: Many utilities want the high leg on the RIGHT-hand (C) position in self-contained meter sockets ≤200 A, then back in the CENTER (B) at the service disconnect.
cards.note: CT-metered services over 200 A avoid it. Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: Most common system in modern commercial buildings, and its usual voltages?
cards.back: 3Ø 4-wire wye: 208Y/120, 480Y/277, 600Y/347 V. Line-to-neutral loads can go on any phase.
cards.note: Primaries are usually delta (only 3 conductors). Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: Name 4 transformer-related causes of unbalanced voltage.
cards.back: Large single-phase loads, open connections at a transformer secondary, open-delta banks, unequal %Z of 1Ø transformers in a 3Ø bank (also unequal/open capacitor banks).
cards.note: Small voltage unbalance = big extra heat in a motor. Textbook Ch. 7.

cards.front: What is an isolation transformer?
cards.back: A 1:1 transformer used only for isolation: blocks spikes/noise, breaks ground loops, feeds sensitive equipment.
cards.note: Often has a grounded electrostatic shield.

cards.front: What grounding does an isolation transformer secondary need?
cards.back: It's a separately derived system (NEC 250.30): system bonding jumper, grounding electrode conductor, supply-side bonding jumper.
cards.note: Without it, a ground fault on the secondary won't trip anything.

cards.front: What is a buck-boost transformer?
cards.back: A small isolating transformer wired as an autotransformer with its LV winding in series with the line, to raise or lower voltage ~5–27%.

cards.front: Why is correct voltage important for motors?
cards.back: Low voltage raises motor current, lowers torque and raises temperature, shortening insulation life.

cards.front: What is an autotransformer?
cards.back: A one-winding transformer: the same winding is both primary and secondary.
cards.note: Most efficient type; the shared section carries only the difference current.

cards.front: Two disadvantages of autotransformers?
cards.back: 1) No isolation between HV and LV sides. 2) If the common winding opens while stepping down, full line voltage appears at the load.

cards.front: What is a Variac?
cards.back: A variable autotransformer: a brush rides on the winding to give adjustable output from 0 to slightly above line voltage.
cards.note: Used in the lab bench supplies.

cards.front: NEC-permitted uses of autotransformers?
cards.back: Systems with a grounded conductor common to both sides; motor starting; theater dimming; lighting ballasts; buck/boost under certain conditions.

cards.front: What is a control transformer?
cards.back: Steps 240/480 V down to 120 V (or 24 V) for control circuits (coils, pilot lights, PLC I/O).

cards.front: Dual-primary control transformer (240 × 480): how are primaries connected for each voltage?
cards.back: 480 V: primaries in SERIES (jumper H2–H3). 240 V: primaries in PARALLEL (H1–H3, H2–H4).
cards.note: Check the jumper drawing on the nameplate before wiring.

cards.front: Why is one side (X2) of a control transformer secondary often grounded?
cards.back: So a ground fault in the control circuit blows the fuse instead of energizing a coil and starting a motor.

cards.front: Neon sign transformer voltages and currents?
cards.back: Primary 120/240 V; secondary 2,000–15,000 V; 30–120 mA. Self air-cooled, mounted in the sign.
cards.note: Current-limiting by design. NEC Art. 600. Lethal despite mA rating.

cards.front: What is a K-rated transformer?
cards.back: One built to withstand extra heating from harmonic currents drawn by non-linear loads.
cards.note: K-1 = linear loads only; common ratings K-4, K-13, K-20.

cards.front: Name 5 loads that produce harmonics.
cards.back: Any 5: switch-mode power supplies (PCs, TVs), VFDs, LED/fluorescent ballasts, UPSs, PV inverters, arc furnaces, welders, solid-state dimmers/heater controls, HVDC converters.

cards.front: Why can the neutral of a 4-wire wye carry more current than the phases?
cards.back: Triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th...) from non-linear loads add in the neutral instead of cancelling.
cards.note: K-rated units often have a double-size neutral.

cards.front: How do you determine what K-rating is needed?
cards.back: Measure K-factor with a power-quality meter with the system fully loaded.

cards.front: What is a no-load tap changer (NLTC), and the key rule for using it?
cards.back: A switch that changes the turns ratio (taps usually in 2½% steps). It must only be moved with the transformer DE-ENERGIZED.
cards.note: Substation load tap changers (LTCs) are different: they work under load.

cards.front: Secondary voltage is too low. Do you move to a higher or lower % primary tap?
cards.back: LOWER % tap (fewer primary turns) raises the output. Higher % tap lowers it.
cards.note: E.g., 95% tap raises output ~5%.

cards.front: What does a transformer pressure relief device do?
cards.back: A spring-loaded valve vents internal pressure from a fault or overheating so the tank doesn't rupture, then reseals. A flag stays up; often has alarm/trip contacts.
cards.note: A tripped PRD means a serious internal event: test before re-energizing.

cards.front: Can harmonics overheat a transformer without tripping its overcurrent device?
cards.back: Yes (NEC 450.3 Informational Note 2). Fixes: oversize the transformer, use K-rated, run separate neutrals for non-linear loads.
cards.note: IEEE C57.110. Textbook Ch. 8.

cards.front: What does a constant-current transformer do, and where is it used?
cards.back: Holds secondary current constant (usually 6.6 A) as load changes. Used on series streetlights and airport runway lighting.
cards.note: Primary typically 2,400 V.

cards.front: Why are series streetlights/runway lights fed from a CCT?
cards.back: Series wiring saves copper, and lamp brightness tracks current closely, so regulating current keeps brightness steady.

cards.front: How does a CCT regulate current mechanically?
cards.back: A movable coil floats; the windings' fields repel. More current pushes them apart, increasing leakage and reducing current. A counterweight and oil dashpot prevent 'hunting'.

cards.front: Why must you never open a live series lighting (CCT) circuit?
cards.back: The regulator drives voltage to maximum trying to keep current flowing: several kV across the opening.

cards.front: In a series lighting circuit, what keeps the circuit closed when a lamp fails?
cards.back: A film cutout or a reactor (reactance coil) at each lamp.

cards.front: What are instrument transformers for?
cards.back: Step high voltage/current down to safe standard values (120 V, 5 A) for meters, relays and SCADA, and isolate those devices from the primary.
cards.note: Small VA, high accuracy.

cards.front: PT vs CT connection and secondary rating?
cards.back: PT: in PARALLEL, 120 V secondary (115 V older). CT: in SERIES, 5 A secondary.

cards.front: The opposite safety rules for PTs and CTs?
cards.back: Never SHORT a PT secondary. Never OPEN a CT secondary.

cards.front: Why must you never short a PT secondary?
cards.back: A PT is a voltage source; a short draws destructive current (slides: primary current could rise ~200×).
cards.note: PT primaries are fused; never remove a ground from an energized PT.

cards.front: Why must PT fuses/switches be opened when working on connected equipment?
cards.back: A PT can backfeed: voltage on its secondary steps up to full primary voltage.

cards.front: Why must you never open the secondary of an energized CT?
cards.back: The CT is driven by primary current. With nothing to oppose the flux, it acts as a step-up transformer: thousands of volts, shock, arcing, insulation and core damage.
cards.note: Short it at the shorting block or test switch first.

cards.front: Standard CT secondary current?
cards.back: 5 A at rated primary current, regardless of primary rating.
cards.note: 1 A secondaries also exist (common outside N. America, long runs).

cards.front: Name 4 CT types.
cards.back: Window/donut/ring, split-core, bar type, wound type, bushing type.
cards.note: Window CTs are less accurate at low ratios than wound CTs.

cards.front: Shortcut for finding the ratio of an X:5 CT?
cards.back: Double the primary number and drop the last zero. 600:5 → 120:1; 2000:5 → 400:1.
cards.note: Works because ÷5 = ×2 ÷10.

cards.front: CT current ratio vs turns ratio?
cards.back: I<sub>S</sub>/I<sub>P</sub> = N<sub>P</sub>/N<sub>S</sub>. A 600:5 window CT has 120 secondary turns.

cards.front: On a multi-ratio CT, what do you do with the unused taps?
cards.back: Leave them OPEN. Don't short them.

cards.front: How does passing the primary through a window CT twice change its ratio?
cards.back: It halves it: 200:5 becomes 100:5. New ratio = nameplate ratio ÷ number of passes.

cards.front: How do you count 'turns' on a window CT?
cards.back: Count passes THROUGH the window, not loops around the outside. One loop around the housing = 2 passes.

cards.front: What is CT burden?
cards.back: Everything connected to the secondary: meters, relays, transducers, and lead wire resistance (VA or ohms).
cards.note: Excess burden reduces accuracy.

cards.front: What is CT saturation, and what is the knee point?
cards.back: Past a point, more primary current gives no more secondary current. The bend in the excitation curve is the knee point.
cards.note: A saturated protection CT under-reports fault current; relay may not trip.

cards.front: Name 4 factors affecting CT accuracy.
cards.back: Burden, accuracy class, rating factor, load, external magnetic fields, temperature, physical configuration, tap selected.

cards.front: How many points should a CT secondary circuit be grounded at?
cards.back: One point only (IEEE C57.13.3). NEC Art. 250 Part X covers instrument transformer grounding.

cards.front: Should spare CTs be stored open or shorted?
cards.back: Shorted, including in storage and shipping.

cards.front: Can you megger a CT secondary with the primary energized?
cards.back: No — not even with no load.

cards.front: What is special about CT test switches?
cards.back: They're make-before-break: a shorting contact closes across the CT leads before the blade opens the meter circuit, so the CT is never open.

cards.front: How does a CT shorting terminal block work?
cards.back: A metal bar runs down the block. Screws through the bar tie terminals to it; one screw always ties it to ground. Screws on a CT's terminals short and ground that CT.

cards.front: CT polarity rule?
cards.back: Current IN on polarity (H1) means current OUT on polarity (X1) at the same instant.
cards.note: CT polarity is always subtractive. Marks: H1/X1 or a dot.

cards.front: What goes wrong if instrument transformer polarity is reversed?
cards.back: Meters read backward, revenue meters record power in the wrong direction, protective relays cover the wrong zone or misoperate.

cards.front: What is a transducer (in metering/SCADA)?
cards.back: A device that converts CT/PT signals (or other physical quantities) into a standard signal, often 4–20 mA or a voltage, for a PLC/RTU/SCADA.

cards.front: SCADA vs HMI?
cards.back: SCADA: the overall supervisory control and data acquisition system talking to RTUs/PLCs. HMI: the operator's graphical screen within it.

cards.front: Purpose of CT saturation testing?
cards.back: Confirms the CT won't saturate at its required burden; also verifies ratio and polarity vs manufacturer data.

cards.front: What is primary (high-voltage) metering?
cards.back: The utility meters on the transformer's HV side with PTs and CTs, often with 15-minute demand registers for kW and kVAR. High demand or low PF raises the rate.
cards.note: Used for single-tenant buildings. Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: Up to what size is a service typically direct-metered (self-contained socket)?
cards.back: 200 A. Larger: 320 A sockets (some utilities) or CT metering; the utility wires CTs to the meter.
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: Describe the AC polarity test.
cards.back: Jumper H1 to the adjacent LV terminal. Apply low AC across H1–H2. Measure H2 to the other adjacent LV terminal. Higher than applied = additive; lower = subtractive.

cards.front: Describe the DC 'kick' polarity test.
cards.back: Analog DC voltmeter on the LV winding. Briefly connect a battery to the HV winding (+ on the lead you call H1). Up-scale kick on MAKE → the LV lead on meter + is X1.
cards.note: The break kick goes the other way; ignore it. Keep hands off: breaking DC on a winding makes a voltage spike.

cards.front: How is %Z measured (short-circuit test)?
cards.back: Short the secondary (ammeter in series), voltmeter on the primary, raise primary voltage from a Variac until rated FLC flows. %Z = that primary voltage ÷ rated × 100.
cards.note: You record the PRIMARY voltage; that is what gives %Z.

cards.front: List the field tests done on a transformer before it is energized.
cards.back: Insulation resistance, turns ratio (TTR), polarity, winding resistance, power factor, CT saturation.
cards.note: Plus oil tests (dielectric, moisture, DGA) on liquid-filled units.

cards.front: Insulation resistance test: what does it measure and how is it done?
cards.back: Leakage through insulation, with a DC megohmmeter: each winding to ground and winding to winding. Higher megohms = less leakage.
cards.note: Record as a baseline; trend it, temperature-corrected. PI and DAR ratios show moisture.

cards.front: TTR test: what does it check?
cards.back: Low-voltage AC test confirming the HV-to-other-windings ratio at no load, on every tap of every winding.
cards.note: Catches shorted turns and wrong tap position. NETA ATS tolerance ≈ 0.5%.

cards.front: Winding resistance test finds what?
cards.back: Loose connections, broken strands, poor tap-changer contacts. Low-resistance DC test; compare phases and factory data, temperature-corrected.
cards.note: Discharge the winding afterward.

cards.front: What does an insulation power factor test measure?
cards.back: Ratio of resistive (loss) current to capacitive current under AC. Rising PF means insulation is degrading (moisture, contamination).
cards.note: Good insulation is well under 1%. Compare to the same unit's history.

cards.front: Why are power factor readings compared to previous readings rather than other equipment?
cards.back: Trend on the same unit is what reveals deterioration; values vary between designs.

cards.front: What is backfeeding a transformer?
cards.back: Energizing it from the 'wrong' side, usually the secondary. It steps the voltage up to full primary voltage on lines thought to be dead.
cards.note: Classic case: a generator plugged into a house without a transfer switch.

cards.front: Before working on a transformer, which sides must be disconnected?
cards.back: BOTH primary and secondary. LOTO, test, and ground as necessary (work between grounds).
cards.note: Any transformer can be backfed.

cards.front: When removing an installed transformer, which leads come off first?
cards.back: The secondary (low-voltage) leads, to remove the backfeed path.

cards.front: What is Askarel, and what precautions apply?
cards.back: A nonflammable synthetic insulating liquid made of PCBs. Banned from new manufacture since the late 1970s. Toxic: avoid contact and fumes; it's hazardous waste.
cards.note: Less fire hazard than oil, but a health hazard.

cards.front: NEC 450.3(B) (≤1,000 V): what are the two overcurrent protection options?
cards.back: 1) Primary only at ≤125% of primary FLC. 2) Primary up to 250% WITH secondary protection at ≤125% of secondary FLC.
cards.note: Next standard size up allowed when ≥9 A. Check your enforced NEC edition.

cards.front: Why is transformer primary protection sized well above 100% of FLC?
cards.back: Inrush: energizing can draw roughly 8–12× FLC for a few cycles while the core magnetizes.
cards.note: Time-delay fuses are common on primaries.

cards.front: Does protecting the transformer protect the secondary conductors?
cards.back: No. Secondary conductors need their own protection under NEC 240.21(C) (10 ft / 25 ft rules, etc.).

cards.front: Two secondary coils in parallel with one reversed: what happens?
cards.back: A dead short across both coils: huge current, blown fuse, damaged windings.

cards.front: Test before making the final parallel connection?
cards.back: Read voltage across the open connection. ~0 V → connect. Voltage present (~double) → polarity wrong, DO NOT connect.
cards.note: Connecting wrong = huge circulating current.

cards.front: In a paralleled bank, one transformer's primary fuse blows. Is its primary dead?
cards.back: No. The other unit backfeeds it through the paralleled secondaries. Its primary stays at full voltage. The good unit may also be overloaded.
cards.note: Treat all primaries in a parallel bank as hot.

cards.front: Why is the center point of a 120/240 V 3-wire secondary grounded?
cards.back: To limit voltage to ground (120 V), provide a fault-current path, and limit voltages from lightning, surges or primary contact.

cards.front: If the 120/240 V neutral were NOT grounded and L1 faulted to ground, what would L2's voltage to ground be?
Open neutral on 120/240 V: what happens to the 120 V loads?
cards.back: Loads on opposite sides go in SERIES across 240 V. Voltage divides by resistance: the lighter load (higher R) gets the HIGHER voltage.
cards.note: Lights going bright/dim when a load cycles = open neutral. Emergency.

cards.front: A transformer is replaced with one of lower %Z. What must you check downstream?
cards.back: Interrupting ratings / SCCR of breakers and fuses (NEC 110.9), the available fault current marking (110.24), and arc-flash labels.

cards.front: Test before closing a delta?
cards.back: Read voltage across the open corner. ~0 V (small reading OK) → close. ~2× winding voltage → a winding is reversed; DO NOT close.
cards.note: Use a meter rated for at least 2× winding voltage.

cards.front: After disconnecting a transformer, why ground the windings?
cards.back: To discharge stored capacitive energy, especially after DC testing. Leave personal grounds on until all work is done.

cards.front: Steps to make a transformer safe to work on?
cards.back: Open both sides, LOTO all sources, test for absence of voltage on both sides, apply grounds, work between grounds.
cards.note: NFPA 70E Art. 120.

cards.front: Safe energization practices?
cards.back: Verify grounds/tools removed, operate remotely if possible, know emergency shutoffs and first aid, wear required PPE, stand clear.

cards.front: Why must transformer cases and metal enclosures (and fences) be grounded?
cards.back: To limit touch voltage from insulation failure and provide a low-impedance fault path so the OCPD trips fast.

cards.front: Three requirements of an effective ground-fault current path?
cards.back: Electrically continuous; able to safely carry any likely fault current for its duration; low impedance to trip the OCPD quickly.

cards.front: How does fault current divide among paths?
cards.back: It uses all available paths, dividing inversely to their impedance, and returns to its source (the transformer secondary).

cards.front: Classic grounding mistake on a new building transformer?
cards.back: Missing system bonding jumper (no fault path), or bonding neutral to ground at both the transformer and downstream panel (neutral current on grounding conductors).
cards.note: Bond at one location only (NEC 250.30).

cards.front: Why did askarel disappear, even though it was nonflammable?
cards.back: It's a PCB mixture, found highly toxic. The Toxic Substances Control Act (1976) and EPA rules ended its use; old units were replaced or refilled.
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: NEC 450.3 overcurrent devices protect what?
cards.back: The transformer only. Conductors supplying or leaving it may need their own protection (Articles 240 and 310).
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: NEC Table 450.3(A) vs 450.3(B)?
cards.back: (A): over 1,000 V, varies with %Z (≤6% or 6–10%), fuse vs breaker, and supervised vs any location. (B): 1,000 V or less (125/167/300% primary-only, or 250% primary with secondary protection).
cards.note: Supervised locations get higher limits.

cards.front: Can a transformer with manufacturer's coordinated thermal overload protection skip primary protection?
cards.back: Yes, if the feeder overcurrent device is set at no more than 6× primary FLC (%Z ≤6%) or 4× (%Z 6–10%).
cards.note: Textbook Fig. 13-2.

cards.front: Name the four grounding/bonding parts of a separately derived system (NEC 250.30(A)).
cards.back: System bonding jumper, supply-side bonding jumper, grounding electrode conductor, grounding electrode.
cards.note: Primary EGC sized per 250.122. Textbook Fig. 13-3.

cards.front: What is a corner-grounded delta?
cards.back: A 3-wire delta secondary with one phase grounded. Phase voltages are unchanged; overcurrent devices generally aren't allowed in the grounded phase.
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: High-leg identification and position rules?
cards.back: Mark it orange (or other effective means) wherever the neutral is present (110.15, 230.56). It's the B phase, in the center position (408.3(E)(1)). Panel warning: 'Caution ___ Phase Has ___ Volts to Ground' (408.3(F)).
cards.note: Also called red leg or wild leg.

cards.front: NEC vs NESC: which applies to the utility's transformer?
cards.back: The NESC applies up to the service point (utility equipment); the NEC applies to premises wiring after it (90.2(D)(5)). The utility sets the service point.
cards.note: Check who furnishes the service conductors before you bid.

cards.front: Panelboards fed through a transformer: where must overcurrent protection be?
cards.back: On the secondary side (408.36(B)). Exception: 2-wire to 2-wire, or 3-wire delta–delta, can be protected by the primary device through the ratio (240.21(C)(1)).
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 12.

cards.front: What protects service conductors before the service disconnect?
cards.back: Only the utility's transformer primary fuses, which protect the utility transformer, not the conductors. Keep service conductors inside buildings short.
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 13.

cards.front: What do NEC 110.24(A) and (B) require?
cards.back: (A) Non-dwelling service equipment field-marked with available fault current and the calculation date. (B) Recalculate and re-mark when changes (e.g., bigger or lower-%Z utility transformer) affect it.
cards.note: 110.16(B), new in 2023: arc-flash label on non-dwelling service/feeder equipment ≥1,000 A.

cards.front: How can a PV inverter or generator create a hazard on the utility primary?
cards.back: By backfeeding through the service transformer: 240 V can appear as 12,000 V or more on the primary. Hence listed transfer switches and utility-interactive (anti-islanding) inverters.
cards.note: Textbook Ch. 16 and 22.

cards.front: 1Ø 2,400–480 V transformer, I<sub>P</sub> = 15 A. Find TTR and I<sub>S</sub>.
480–120 V (4:1) transformer. 240 V is applied to the primary. Secondary voltage?
cards.note: The output is always proportional to the input.

cards.front: 480–120 V (4:1) transformer. 240 V is applied to the SECONDARY. What appears on the primary?
cards.note: The ratio is fixed and works both directions. That's how backfeed happens.

cards.front: Primary taps: 1,200 turns (240 V), 1,040 turns (208 V), 600 turns (120 V); secondary 120 turns, 24 V. Using the 1,040 tap, what is the ratio and primary voltage?
A 2:1 transformer is fed 438 V instead of 480 V. Output?
cards.back: 219 V (not 240 V). A transformer can't correct low supply voltage; pick a tap that matches the actual supply.

cards.front: 1Ø 25 kVA, 240–120 V. Primary and secondary FLC?
cards.note: kVA primary = kVA secondary.

cards.front: 1Ø 2,000 kVA, 12 kV–2.4 kV. Primary and secondary FLC?
A 50 kW load at PF 0.85 needs what size transformer?
cards.back: VA = W ÷ PF = 50,000 ÷ 0.85 = 58.8 kVA → next standard size up: 75 kVA.
cards.note: Never round down.

cards.front: Clamp-on: 200 A on each leg of a 240 V single-phase 60 kVA transformer. Load and % loaded?
Unbalanced 120/240 V: L1 = 20 A, L2 = 30 A, N = 10 A. kVA load?
cards.back: (20 + 30) × 120 V = 6 kVA. Ignore the neutral current.
cards.note: Each 120 V half delivers its line current at 120 V.

cards.front: A 65 °C rise transformer in a 40 °C ambient: average max winding temperature?
cards.back: 40 + 65 = 105 °C. The hot spot runs higher still (insulation class covers it).

cards.front: Polarity test on a 4:1 unit with 120 V applied. What do additive and subtractive read?
cards.back: Secondary = 30 V. Additive: 120 + 30 = 150 V. Subtractive: 120 − 30 = 90 V.

cards.front: 50 kVA and 100 kVA transformers in parallel share a 75 kVA load. How much does each carry?
cards.note: Assumes matched %Z.

cards.front: 25 kVA 120/240 V: side 1 = 167 A, side 2 = 42 A. How loaded is each half?
cards.back: Each half is rated 12.5 kVA = 104 A. Side 1: 167/104 = 160% (60% overloaded). Side 2: 42/104 = 40% loaded.
cards.note: Total is exactly 25 kVA, yet one winding is overloaded.

cards.front: 75 kVA 12,500–120/240 V. Loads: 6 kVA @240 V, 3 kVA @120 V on L1 side, 3.6 kVA @120 V on L2 side. Find L1, L2, N and primary currents.
cards.back: 240 V load 25 A; 3 kVA = 25 A; 3.6 kVA = 30 A. L1 = 50 A, L2 = 55 A, N = 5 A. Primary ≈ 12,600 ÷ 12,500 ≈ 1.0 A. Loaded 16.8%.

cards.front: Open neutral: 3 kVA and 3.6 kVA 120 V loads on opposite sides. Voltage on each?
cards.back: R = 4.8 Ω and 4.0 Ω; I = 240 ÷ 8.8 = 27.3 A. 3 kVA load: 131 V. 3.6 kVA load: 109 V.
cards.note: The smaller load gets the higher voltage.

cards.front: A 480 V transformer has 5 %Z. At what voltage does FLA flow with the secondary shorted, and what is the fault current at 480 V?
cards.back: 0.05 × 480 = 24 V. At 480 V the fault current is 480/24 = 20 × FLA.

cards.front: 25 kVA, 240 V, 2 %Z. Maximum fault current?
Boost vs buck connection: 120 V supply, 24 V winding?
cards.back: Boost (additive): 120 + 24 = 144 V. Buck (subtractive): 120 − 24 = 96 V.

cards.front: A 1 kVA buck-boost unit (24 V secondary) boosts 120 V to 144 V. About how much load can it feed?
cards.back: Secondary current limit = 1,000 ÷ 24 = 41.7 A. Load ≈ 41.7 × 144 ≈ 6 kVA.
cards.note: It only carries the 'difference' power. Size by load current.

cards.front: A 600:5 CT has 300 A in the primary. Secondary current?
600:5 multi-ratio CT (X1–X2 20, X2–X3 10, X3–X4 50, X4–X5 40 turns). Which taps give 150:5?
cards.back: 150:5 = 30:1 → 20 + 10 → X1–X3. Leave other taps open.

cards.front: Tapped CT: X1–X2 = 40, X1–X3 = 60, X1–X4 = 160, X1–X5 = 240 turns. Which taps give 500:5?
200:5 CT with 3 and with 4 passes?
2500/5 donut CT. How many passes for a 125:1 ratio?
Two 800:5 CTs, 400 A primary, secondaries share a middle meter. When does the middle meter read 0 A?
cards.back: When the two CTs' 2.5 A secondary currents meet head-on in the shared meter: they cancel there and circulate through the outer meters (2.5 A each).
cards.note: Trace current out of X1 and back to its own X2 by the lowest-impedance path.

cards.front: 50 kVA, 480 V → 208Y/120 V 3Ø. Primary FLC, 125% primary fuse, and max primary fuse (with secondary protection)?
cards.back: FLC = 50,000 ÷ (480 × 1.732) = 60 A. 125% = 75 A → next standard 80 A dual-element fuses (100 A switch). Max = 60 × 250% = 150 A.
cards.note: Textbook Fig. 13-3.

cards.front: Same 50 kVA, 480–208Y/120 V transformer: secondary FLC and overcurrent device?
cards.back: FLC = 50,000 ÷ (208 × 1.732) = 139 A. ×125% = 174 A → 175 A fuses or breaker. It also protects the panel (408.36) and secondary conductors (240.21(C)).
cards.note: Textbook Fig. 13-3.

cards.front: Two 100 kVA transformers in open delta: capacity?
cards.note: 86.6% of the two nameplates, 57.7% of a full 3-unit delta.

cards.front: 225 kVA, 208Y/120 V, 2 %Z (infinite primary, book method). Fault current at the terminals?
cards.note: 1% → 69,444 A; 4% → 17,363 A. Textbook Problem 1, Ch. 18.
